# Genus-3 Lefschetz pencils on torus bundles

**Authors:** Evan Huang Address: Department of Mathematics Princeton University Princeton, NJ, 08544 Email address: evan.huang@princeton.edu

## Abstract

We use the breeding technique to construct genus-3 Lefschetz pencils for which the total spaces have $c_{1}=0$ . We compute the fundamental groups of our Lefschetz pencils and identify them with the fundamental groups of certain torus bundles over tori. Using work of Friedl and Vidussi, the total spaces of our pencils are homeomorphic to torus bundles over tori. These bundles do not admit sections.

## Introduction

The notion of Kodaira dimension can be extended from Kähler surfaces to closed symplectic 4-manifolds [7], and takes values in $\{-\infty,0,1,2\}$ . While the definition of Kodaira dimension $\kappa$ depends on a the symplectic form, it turns out to be a smooth invariant. Manifolds with $\kappa=-\infty$ are completely classified: they are precisely the rational and ruled surfaces (and their blowups) [8].

Symplectic 4-manifolds with $\kappa=0$ are called symplectic Calabi-Yau surfaces (SCYs), and they are characterized by having a minimal model with torsion canonical class. Minimal SCYs are known to have the rational homology type of the K3 surface, Enriques surface, or a torus bundle over a torus [7], [1]. There is a folklore conjecture that every minimal SCY with $b_{1}>0$ is diffeomorphic to some torus bundle over a torus.

One way of constructing SCYs is to find a Lefschetz pencil with the right number of base points or equivalently, a Lefschetz fibration with the right number of disjoint $(-1)$ -sections [5]. Baykur [6] constructed a family of SCYs using genus-3 pencils and showed that his examples cover all possible integral homology types of torus bundles over tori. In addition, Baykur showed that one of his SCYs was homeomorphic to $T^{4}$ .

Going the other way, Smith showed that if $X$ is the total space of a torus bundle over a torus that has a section, then $X$ admits a genus-3 Lefschetz pencil with 4 base points [11]. In [3], Hamada-Hayano worked out the vanishing cycles of Smith’s construction in the case $X=T^{4}$ and showed this pencil to be equivalent to Baykur’s. They also constructed, for each torus bundle $X$ with a section, a genus-3 pencil on a SCY homeomorphic to $X$ .

In this paper, we use genus-3 pencils to construct SCYs that are homeomorphic to torus bundles over tori without sections.

## 1. Torus bundles over tori

We start by recalling some facts about torus bundles from [10]. Given $A,B\in\GL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ with $AB=BA$ and integers $m,n$ , there is a $T^{2}$ -bundle over $T^{2}$ denoted $M(A,B;m,n)$ , where $(A,B)$ is the monodromy of the bundle and $(m,n)$ represents the obstruction to having a section. Every $T^{2}$ -bundle over $T^{2}$ is isomorphic to some $M(A,B;m,n)$ , and in addition, we can assume $B=\pm I$ . More precisely, every $T^{2}$ -bundle over $T^{2}$ is isomorphic to some $M(A,I;m,n)$ or $M(A,-I;m,n)$ .

#### Proposition 1.1.

([10], Section 1) Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix},B=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&s\end{pmatrix}\in\GL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ with $AB=BA$ and $m,n\in\mathbf{Z}$ . Put $M=M(A,B;m,n)$ . The homotopy exact sequence of a fiber bundle gives the following short exact sequence of groups:

$$ 1\to\pi_{1}F\to\pi_{1}M\to\pi_{1}S\to 1. $$

$\pi_{1}M$ is generated by $\alpha,\beta,\sigma,\tau$ with the relations

$$ \displaystyle\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma \displaystyle\alpha^{-1}\sigma\alpha=\sigma^{a}\tau^{c} \displaystyle\beta^{-1}\sigma\beta=\sigma^{p}\tau^{r} \displaystyle\alpha\beta\alpha^{-1}\beta^{-1}=\sigma^{m}\tau^{n} \displaystyle\alpha^{-1}\tau\alpha=\sigma^{b}\tau^{d} \displaystyle\beta^{-1}\tau\beta=\sigma^{q}\tau^{s}. $$

Moreover, $\sigma,\tau$ come from the inclusion $\pi_{1}F\to\pi_{1}M$ and generate $\pi_{1}F$ , and under the projection $\pi_{1}M\to\pi_{1}S$ , $\alpha,\beta$ map to generators.

#### Proposition 1.2.

Let $M=M(A,B;m,n)$ , with $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix},B=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&s\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ . Then $M$ has a section if and only if $\binom{m}{n}\in\langle A-I,B-I\rangle$ , the span of the columns of $A-I$ and $B-I$ .

#### Proof.

We will use the presentation for $\pi_{1}M$ given in Proposition 1.1. From the relations between $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ , we see that $\alpha^{-1}\sigma^{d}\alpha=\sigma^{ad}\tau^{cd}$ and $\alpha^{-1}\tau^{-c}\alpha=\sigma^{-bc}\tau^{-cd}$ . Putting these together gives

$$ \alpha^{-1}\sigma^{d}\tau^{-c}\alpha=\sigma^{ad-bc}=\sigma. $$

Hence $\alpha\sigma\alpha^{-1}=\sigma^{d}\tau^{-c}$ . Similarly, we can write $\alpha\tau\alpha^{-1},\beta\sigma\beta^{-1}$ , and $\beta\tau\beta^{-1}$ in terms of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ . Also recall that $\alpha\beta=\sigma^{m}\tau^{n}\beta\alpha$ .

Note that every element in $\pi_{1}M$ can be written in the form $\sigma^{x}\tau^{y}\beta^{w}\alpha^{z}$ . Given some product of generators, we can use the above observations to move all the $\alpha$ ’s to the right (at the expense of picking up extra $\sigma$ ’s and $\tau$ ’s), then move all the $\beta$ ’s to the right.

Now suppose $M$ has a section. This induces a section $f:\pi_{1}S\to\pi_{1}M$ in the short exact sequence (1). Using our above observations and the fact that $f$ is a section, we see that $f(\alpha)=\sigma^{x}\tau^{y}\alpha$ and $f(\beta)=\sigma^{w}\tau^{z}\beta$ . Moreover, since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ commute in $\pi_{1}S$ , $f(\alpha)$ and $f(\beta)$ must commute in $\pi_{1}M$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle(\sigma^{x}\tau^{y}\alpha)(\sigma^{w}\tau^{z}\beta)=(\sigma^{w}\tau^{z}\beta)(\sigma^{x}\tau^{y}\alpha) \displaystyle\sigma^{x}\tau^{y}(\sigma^{d}\tau^{-c})^{w}(\sigma^{-b}\tau^{a})^{z}\alpha\beta=\sigma^{w}\tau^{z}(\sigma^{s}\tau^{-r})^{x}(\sigma^{-q}\tau^{p})^{y}\beta\alpha \displaystyle\alpha\beta\alpha^{-1}\beta^{-1}=\sigma^{w}\tau^{z}(\sigma^{s}\tau^{-r})^{x}(\sigma^{-q}\tau^{p})^{y}\sigma^{-x}\tau^{-y}(\sigma^{d}\tau^{-c})^{-w}(\sigma^{-b}\tau^{a})^{-z} \displaystyle\sigma^{m}\tau^{n}=\sigma^{w}\tau^{z}(\sigma^{s}\tau^{-r})^{x}(\sigma^{-q}\tau^{p})^{y}\sigma^{-x}\tau^{-y}(\sigma^{d}\tau^{-c})^{-w}(\sigma^{-b}\tau^{a})^{-z}. $$

This equation now only involves $\sigma$ ’s and $\tau$ ’s, and since $\pi_{1}F\to\pi_{1}M$ is an inclusion, we see that the powers of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ must match up. Writing $\binom{k}{l}$ to denote $\sigma^{k}\tau^{l}$ , the above equation simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}m\\
n\end{pmatrix} \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}w\\
z\end{pmatrix}+x\begin{pmatrix}s\\
-r\end{pmatrix}+y\begin{pmatrix}-q\\
p\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}x\\

-c\end{pmatrix}-z\begin{pmatrix}-b\\

Conversely, if $\binom{m}{n}\in\langle A-I,B-I\rangle$ , then according to Proposition 2(3) of [10], $M(A,B;m,n)$ is isomorphic to $M(A,B;0,0)$ as bundles, and $M(A,B;0,0)$ has a section by construction. ∎

## 2. Symplectic Calabi-Yaus

We now recall some facts about the symplectic Kodaira dimension, based on [7]. Given a symplectic manifold $(X,\omega)$ , let $(X_{0},\omega_{0})$ be a minimal model with canonical class $K_{X_{0}}$ . The symplectic Kodaira dimension $\kappa(X,\omega)$ is defined to be either $-\infty,0,1$ , or $2$ , depending on the signs of $K_{X_{0}}\cdot[\omega_{0}]$ and $K_{X_{0}}^{2}$ . The definition of $\kappa$ is independent of the minimal model and of the particular symplectic form and is hence a smooth invariant.

#### Definition 2.1.

A symplectic 4-manifold $X$ is called a symplectic Calabi-Yau surface, or SCY for short, if $\kappa(X)=0$ . As observed by Li ([7] Proposition 2.4), if $X_{0}$ is a minimal model of $X$ and $K_{X_{0}}$ its canonical class, then $\kappa=0$ is equivalent to saying that $K_{X_{0}}$ is torsion in $H^{2}(X_{0};\mathbf{Z})$ .

#### Remark 2.2.

Note that if $X$ is a symplectic 4-manifold with torsion canonical class $K$ , then either $K$ is actually trivial or $X$ is an integral homology Enriques surface (in which case $K$ has order two); see Proposition 6.3 in [7]. In this paper, all SCYs under consideration have $b_{1}\geq 2$ (since $b_{1}\geq 2$ for torus bundles; see [10], Proposition 1), which rules out integral homology Enriques surfaces and their blowups, so our SCYs all have minimal models with $K=0$ .

Observe that if $X$ is a SCY and $X=X_{0}\#n\overline{\mathbf{C}P^{2}}$ , with $X_{0}$ minimal, then $0=c_{1}^{2}(X_{0})=c_{1}^{2}(X)+n$ . Hence if $X$ is a SCY and $c_{1}^{2}(X)=0$ , then $X$ is already minimal. In this paper, all our SCYs will have $c_{1}^{2}=0$ by construction, and thus our SCYs are minimal. Combining this with our previous observation, all our SCYs have $K=0$ . This will be implicit every time we invoke Corollary 2.1.

The following gives a good source of SCYs:

#### Proposition 2.1.

([6], Proposition 1; see also [5], Theorem 4.1) Suppose $(X,f)$ is a genus- $g$ Lefschetz pencil with $b$ base points and $X$ is not rational or ruled. Then $X$ is a SCY or a rational homology Enriques surface if and only if $b=2g-2$ .

It turns out that a large class of SCYs are determined up to homeomorphism by their fundamental group. We recall the following from [2] (note that in their language, a SCY is required to have $K=0$ , which excludes nonminimal 4-manifolds and integral homology Enriques surfaces):

#### Definition 2.3.

Let $G$ be a finitely-presented group. If $G=\pi_{1}X$ for some SCY $X$ such that $K_{X}=0$ , then we say that $G$ is a SCY group.

#### Theorem 2.4.

([2], Corollary 3.3) Let $X$ be a SCY with $K_{X}=0$ , and assume further that $X$ is an infrasolvmanifold. If $Y$ is a SCY with $K_{Y}=0$ and $\pi_{1}Y\cong\pi_{1}X$ , then $X$ and $Y$ are homeomorphic.

Note that all $T^{2}$ -bundles over $T^{2}$ are SCYs with $K=0$ and are also infrasolvmanifolds [7], [2]. Thus we get the following corollary, which will tell us the homeomorphism types of the SCYs we construct:

#### Corollary 2.1.

Let $X$ be a SCY with $K_{X}=0$ . If $\pi_{1}X$ is isomorphic to $\pi_{1}M(A,B;m,n)$ , then $X$ is homeomorphic to $M(A,B;m,n)$ .

#### Remark 2.5.

These arguments are not new. Baykur and Hamada-Hayano used this line of reasoning to identify homeomorphism types in [6], [3].

## 3. Semidirect products

Given a matrix $A\in\GL(3,\mathbf{Z})$ , we get an action $\mathbf{Z}\curvearrowright\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ , which in turn defines a semidirect product $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}$ .

#### Proposition 3.1.

If $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\GL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ and $M=M(A,I;m,n)$ , then $\pi_{1}M\cong\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{\tilde{A}}\mathbf{Z}$ , where

$$ \tilde{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&-ma-nb\\
c&d&-mc-nd\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

#### Proof.

Using the presentation of $\pi_{1}M$ given in Proposition 1.1, we see that $\sigma,\tau$ , and $\beta$ all commute. Observe that $\alpha\beta\alpha^{-1}\beta^{-1}=\sigma^{m}\tau^{n}$ implies

$$ \displaystyle\alpha\beta\alpha^{-1} \displaystyle=\sigma^{m}\tau^{n}\beta \displaystyle\beta \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\sigma^{m}\tau^{n}\beta\alpha \displaystyle=(\sigma^{a}\tau^{c})^{m}(\sigma^{b}\tau^{d})^{n}\alpha^{-1}\beta\alpha, $$

and hence $\alpha^{-1}\beta\alpha=\sigma^{-ma-nb}\tau^{-mc-nd}\beta$ . Thus $\pi_{1}M$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes\mathbf{Z}$ , where the $\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ subgroup is generated by $\sigma,\tau,\beta$ and the $\mathbf{Z}$ -action by $\alpha$ is specified by

$$ \alpha^{-1}\sigma\alpha=\sigma^{a}\tau^{c},\;\;\alpha^{-1}\tau\alpha=\sigma^{b}\tau^{d},\;\;\alpha^{-1}\beta\alpha=\sigma^{-ma-nb}\tau^{-mc-nd}\beta. $$

∎

#### Remark 3.1.

If we are given $\tilde{A}$ as

$$ \tilde{A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&x\\
c&d&y\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, $$

then we have $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{\tilde{A}}\mathbf{Z}\cong\pi_{1}M(A,I;m,n)$ , with $m,n$ given by

$$ \begin{pmatrix}m\\
n\end{pmatrix}=-A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}x\\
y\end{pmatrix}. $$

#### Lemma 3.1.

Let $A,P\in\GL(3,\mathbf{Z})$ and set $B=PAP^{-1}$ . Then

$$ \mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}\cong\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{B}\mathbf{Z}. $$

#### Proof.

Define $\phi:\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{B}\mathbf{Z}$ by $\phi(v,n)=(Pv,n)$ . In $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{B}\mathbf{Z}$ , we have

$$ \begin{split}\phi(v,n)\phi(w,m)&=(Pv,n)(Pw,m)\\
&=(Pv+B^{n}Pw,n+m)\\
&=(Pv+PA^{n}w,n+m)\\
&=\phi(v+A^{n}w,n+m)\\
&=\phi((v,n)(w,m)),\end{split} $$

so $\phi$ is a homomorphism. $\phi^{-1}(v,n)=(P^{-1}v,n)$ is the inverse, so $\phi$ is an isomorphism. ∎

## 4. Baykur’s genus-3 pencils on SCYs

In [6], Baykur constructed genus-3 pencils on SCYs by breeding two copies of Matsumoto’s genus-2 relation. The genus-3 pencils depend on a mapping class $\phi$ in $\Mod(\Sigma_{3}^{4})$ that fixes some set of curves on $\Sigma_{3}^{4}$ - this mapping class is used to conjugate one of the Matsumoto relations (the unprimed curves in Baykur’s notation). When $\phi$ is the identity, the vanishing cycles are written in terms of the standard generators of $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ in [6], equations (48)-(59). A straightforward computation shows that the total space $X$ of the Lefschetz pencil has $\pi_{1}(X)=\mathbf{Z}^{4}$ . Corollary 2.1 then implies that $X$ is homeomorphic to the 4-torus $T^{4}$ (the trivial $T^{2}$ -bundle over $T^{2}$ with monodromy $(A,B)=(I,I)$ and obstruction class $(0,0)$ ).

By taking $\phi=t_{b_{1}}^{l}t_{a_{3}}^{k}$ (see [6], Figure 4 for these curves), Baykur obtains a family $X_{l,k}$ of SCYs that realizes all possible integral homology types of SCYs with $b_{1}>0$ . As a warm-up for later computations, we will show that the $X_{l,k}$ are all homeomorphic to $T^{2}$ -bundles over $T^{2}$ . More precisely,

#### Theorem 4.1.

$X_{l,k}$ is homeomorphic to $M(T,I;0,0)$ , where

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}lk+1&l\\
k&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

These torus bundles all have sections.

#### Proof.

$\pi_{1}(X_{l,k})$ is obtained from $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ by dividing out all the vanishing cycles. We use the standard generators of $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ , as in [6], Figure 4. We start with the primed curves coming from the unconjugated embedding of Matsumoto’s relation, given in [6], equations (54)-(59):

$$ a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}a_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}^{2}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{2}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}^{2}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ [a_{1},b_{1}][a_{2},b_{2}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

(See [6], Figure 7 for these curves). Using ( $B_{0}^{\prime}$ ) in ( $A_{0}^{\prime}$ ), we see that $a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{2}=1$ , so $[a_{3},b_{2}]=1$ . Using this, we commute some $a_{3}$ ’s and $b_{2}$ ’s in ( $A_{1}^{\prime}$ ) and ( $A_{2}^{\prime}$ ):

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}^{2}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

Cancelling off the $a_{3}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{2}^{-1}$ on the right side of both gives $a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}=b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}$ . Thus $a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}=b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}$ , and using ( $B_{0}^{\prime}$ ) we get $a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}=b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}$ , so $[a_{1},b_{1}]=1$ .

We modify ( $B_{2}^{\prime}$ ) by first commuting $a_{3}$ and $b_{2}$ , then using ( $B_{0}^{\prime}$ ), then commuting $a_{1}$ and $b_{1}$ :

$$ \begin{split}1&=b_{1}a_{2}a_{3}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}\\
&=b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}\\
&=b_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}a_{2}^{-1}.\end{split} $$

So far, our relations simplify to

$$ a_{1}=a_{2}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1} $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}^{2}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}=a_{2}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1} $$

$$ [a_{3},b_{2}]=1 $$

$$ [a_{1},b_{1}]=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ [a_{2},b_{2}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

Using ( $B_{0}^{\prime}$ ) and ( $B_{2}^{\prime}$ ) in ( $A_{1}^{\prime}$ ), we see that

$$ 1=[a_{2}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1},a_{2}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}]=a_{2}[a_{3}^{-1},b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}]a_{2}^{-1}, $$

so $a_{3}$ commutes with $b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}$ . Since $a_{3}$ already commutes with $b_{2}$ by ( $A_{0}^{\prime}$ ), it follows that $a_{3}$ commutes with $b_{3}$ . Thus ( $A_{1}^{\prime}$ ) is equivalent to $[a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ and ( $\Sigma$ ) becomes $[a_{2},b_{2}]=1$ . We can modify ( $B_{1}^{\prime}$ ) using our commutators and ( $B_{0}^{\prime}$ ):

$$ \begin{split}1&=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}\\
&=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}\\
&=b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}.\end{split} $$

This is the same as ( $B_{2}^{\prime}$ ), so we can eliminate ( $B_{1}^{\prime}$ ). Lastly, we modify ( $A_{2}^{\prime}$ ) using our commutators and ( $B_{2}^{\prime}$ ):

$$ \begin{split}1&=a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}\\
&=b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{2},\end{split} $$

so $b_{2}b_{3}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}=1$ . That is, $[b_{2},b_{3}]=1$ . Our relations have been simplified to:

$$ a_{1}=a_{2}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{1}=a_{2}b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1} $$

$$ [a_{3},b_{2}]=1 $$

$$ [a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

$$ [b_{2},b_{3}]=1 $$

$$ [a_{2},b_{2}]=1 $$

We now determine the relations coming from the unprimed curves (the conjugated embedding of Matsumoto’s relation). Again, see [6], Figure 7 for these curves. The induced action of $t_{b_{1}}$ on $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ sends $a_{1}$ to $a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}$ and fixes all other generators, and the induced action of $t_{a_{3}}$ on $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ sends $b_{3}$ to $b_{3}a_{3}$ and fixes all other generators. It follows that the induced action of $\phi=t_{b_{1}}^{l}t_{a_{3}}^{k}$ on $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ is given by

$$ \phi(a_{1})=a_{1}b_{1}^{-l},\;\;\phi(b_{3})=b_{3}a_{3}^{k}, $$

and all other generators are fixed. Combining this with (48)-(53) in [6], we get the additional relations in $\pi_{1}(X_{l,k})$ :

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-l}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-l-1}a_{2}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}^{-k+1}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}^{-k}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}[a_{3},b_{3}]a_{1}b_{1}^{-l}[b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}[a_{3},b_{3}]a_{1}b_{1}^{-l-1}a_{2}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}[b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}a_{3}^{-k+1}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}[a_{3},b_{3}]a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}([b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2})^{2}a_{3}^{-k}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

Using the commutators in ( $A_{0}^{\prime}$ ), ( $A_{1}^{\prime}$ ), ( $A_{2}^{\prime}$ ), and ( $\Sigma$ ) gives:

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-l}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-l-1}b_{2}a_{3}^{-k+1}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}a_{3}^{-k}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-l}b_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-l-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{3}^{-k+1}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}^{2}a_{3}^{-k}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

In ( $A_{1}$ ) we can commute one power of $b_{2}$ to the very right using ( $A_{0}^{\prime}$ ) and ( $\Sigma$ ), and this gives ( $B_{1}$ ), so we can get rid of ( $A_{1}$ ). Likewise, in ( $A_{2}$ ) we can commute one power of $b_{2}$ to the very right and this gives ( $B_{2}$ ), so we can get rid of ( $A_{2}$ ). In ( $A_{0}$ ) we can commute $b_{2}$ and $a_{3}$ and recognize this as ( $B_{0}$ ), so ( $A_{0}$ ) can be eliminated. Finally, note that ( $B_{0}$ ), ( $B_{2}$ ), and ( $A_{1}^{\prime}$ ) imply ( $B_{1}$ ).

The only remaining relations are ( $B_{0}$ ) and ( $B_{2}$ ).Using ( $B_{0}^{\prime}$ ) and ( $B_{2}^{\prime}$ ) to eliminate the generators $a_{1},b_{1}$ in ( $B_{0}$ ) and ( $B_{2}$ ) shows that $\pi_{1}(X_{l,k})$ is generated by $a_{2},b_{2},a_{3},b_{3}$ with the relations

$$ a_{2}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{-l}b_{3}^{l}a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}b_{3}a_{2}^{-1}b_{2}a_{3}^{-k}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ [a_{3},b_{2}]=1 $$

$$ [a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

$$ [b_{2},b_{3}]=1 $$

$$ [a_{2},b_{2}]=1 $$

( $B_{0}$ ) can be rearranged to $a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}a_{2}=a_{3}b_{2}^{l}b_{3}^{-l}$ . Cancelling the $b_{2}$ ’s in ( $B_{2}$ ) and rearranging gives

$$ \begin{split}a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}^{-k}b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}&=b_{3}^{-1}\\
(a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}a_{2})^{-k}a_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}&=b_{3}^{-1}\\
a_{3}^{-k}b_{2}^{-lk}b_{3}^{lk}a_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}&=b_{3}^{-1}\\
a_{2}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}&=a_{3}^{k}b_{2}^{lk}b_{3}^{-lk-1}\\
a_{2}^{-1}b_{3}a_{2}&=a_{3}^{-k}b_{2}^{-lk}b_{3}^{lk+1}\end{split} $$

We are done simplifying the relations. The final presentation for $\pi_{1}(X_{l,k})$ is

$$ \pi_{1}(X_{l,k})=\langle a_{2},b_{2},a_{3},b_{3}|a_{2}^{-1}a_{3}a_{2}=b_{3}^{-l}a_{3}b_{2}^{l},a_{2}^{-1}b_{3}a_{2}=b_{3}^{lk+1}a_{3}^{-k}b_{2}^{-lk},\\
[a_{3},b_{2}]=1,[a_{3},b_{3}]=1,[b_{2},b_{3}]=1,[a_{2},b_{2}]=1\rangle. $$

This is precisely the presentation for a semidirect product $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}$ , with $\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ generated by the ordered basis $\{b_{3},a_{3},b_{2}\}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ generated by $a_{2}$ , and the action of $a_{2}$ on $\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ given by

$$ A=\begin{pmatrix}lk+1&-l&0\\
-k&1&0\\
-lk&l&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

Set

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\
0&-1&0\\
1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\in\GL(3,\mathbf{Z}). $$

We get that

$$ B=PAP^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}lk+1&l&0\\
k&1&0\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

By Lemma 3.1, $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}\cong\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{B}\mathbf{Z}$ , and by Proposition 3.1, $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{B}\mathbf{Z}\cong\pi_{1}(M(T,I;0,0))$ with

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}lk+1&l\\
k&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

Baykur computed that $e(X_{l,k})=\sigma(X_{l,k})=0$ , so $c_{1}^{2}(X_{l,k})=0$ . Moreover, since we identified $\pi_{1}(X_{l,k})$ with that of a torus bundle, $b_{1}(X_{l,k})\geq 2$ . It follows from Corollary 2.1 and Remark 2.2 that $X_{l,k}$ is homeomorphic to $M(T,I;0,0)$ . These torus bundles all have sections by Proposition 1.2. ∎

## 5. More genus-3 pencils

In this section, we will use the same breeding technique of [6] to produce genus-3 pencils on a family of SCYs, and by identifying the resulting fundamental groups as those arising from torus bundles, we know the homeomorphism type of our SCYs. Moreover, many of the torus bundles in this family do not have sections.

Recall equation (5-2) in [3], which is a modification of Matsumoto’s $(6,2)$ relation in $\Sigma_{2}^{4}$ . We embed $\Sigma_{2}^{4}$ in $\Sigma_{3}^{4}$ as in [3], Figure 14 (d)-(f), giving the relation

$$ t_{d_{7}}t_{d_{8}}t_{d_{9}}t_{d_{10}}t_{d_{11}}t_{d_{12}}=t_{\delta_{3}}t_{\delta_{4}}t_{s_{1}}t_{s_{2}}t_{s_{3}}^{-1}t_{s_{4}}^{-1}. $$

Also recall equation (44) in [6], which is another modification of Matsumoto’s $(6,2)$ relation in $\Sigma_{2}^{4}$ . We embed $\Sigma_{2}^{4}$ in $\Sigma_{3}^{4}$ as in [6], left half of Figure 7, giving the relation (45) in [6]:

$$ t_{B_{0}}t_{B_{1}}t_{B_{2}}t_{A_{0}}t_{A_{1}}t_{A_{2}}=t_{\partial_{1}}t_{\partial_{2}}t_{C_{1}^{\prime}}t_{C_{2}^{\prime}}t_{C_{1}}^{-1}t_{C_{2}}^{-1}. $$

Combining the notation used in [3] and [6], we see that $\partial_{1}=\delta_{1}$ , $\partial_{2}=\delta_{2}$ , $C_{1}=s_{2}$ , $C_{2}=s_{1}$ , $C_{1}^{\prime}=s_{4}$ , and $C_{2}^{\prime}=s_{3}$ . Given any mapping class $\phi\in\Mod(\Sigma_{3}^{4})$ that fixes $s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}$ , and $s_{4}$ , we can breed the relations (3) and (4) to get the positive factorization

$$ t_{d_{7}}t_{d_{8}}t_{d_{9}}t_{d_{10}}t_{d_{11}}t_{d_{12}}t_{\phi(B_{0})}t_{\phi(B_{1})}t_{\phi(B_{2})}t_{\phi(A_{0})}t_{\phi(A_{1})}t_{\phi(A_{2})}=t_{\delta_{1}}t_{\delta_{2}}t_{\delta_{3}}t_{\delta_{4}}. $$

Let us call the total space of the Lefschetz pencil associated to this factorization $X_{\phi}$ .

We first determine the relations in $\pi_{1}$ coming from the vanishing cycles $d_{7},\dots,d_{12}$ . Writing them in terms of the standard generators of $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ ([6], Figure 4), we get the following relations:

$$ [b_{3},a_{3}]a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1 $$

In ( $d_{9}$ ), moving the $a_{3}$ to the front and comparing this to ( $d_{8}$ ), we see that

$$ a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}=a_{2}. $$

Let’s replace ( $d_{8}$ ) with ( $d_{8}^{\prime}$ ), keeping all other relations the same. Using ( $d_{8}^{\prime}$ ), we see that ( $d_{7}$ ) becomes $[b_{3},a_{3}]=1$ . Now using $[b_{3},a_{3}]=1$ , we can cancel the $a_{3}$ ’s in ( $d_{9}$ ) to get $b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}=1$ . So far, relations ( $d_{10}$ )-( $d_{12}$ ) remain unchanged and relations ( $d_{7}$ )-( $d_{9}$ ) now read

$$ [a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

$$ a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}=a_{2} $$

$$ b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}=1 $$

Using $[a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ in ( $d_{10}$ ), we get $b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1$ . Now use ( $d_{8}^{\prime}$ ) to see that $b_{2}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1$ . Thus ( $d_{10}$ ) has become $[b_{2},a_{3}]=1$ . Now we work on ( $d_{11}$ ): use $[a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ and $[b_{2},a_{3}]=1$ to cancel and commute the $a_{3}$ ’s: $b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{2}a_{3}b_{2}^{-1}=1$ . Use ( $d_{8}^{\prime}$ ) to rewrite this as $b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}=1$ . Finally, use ( $d_{9}$ ) to write this as $b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}b_{3}b_{2}^{-1}=1$ . At this point, we have simplified ( $d_{10}$ ) and ( $d_{11}$ ) to

$$ [b_{2},a_{3}]=1 $$

$$ [b_{2},b_{3}]=1 $$

It turns out ( $d_{12}$ ) is redundant: using $[a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ to cancel the $a_{3}$ ’s gives $b_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}=1$ . Now using $[b_{2},b_{3}]=1$ to cancel the $b_{2}$ ’s gives ( $d_{9}$ ).

Rewrite ( $d_{8}^{\prime}$ ) and ( $d_{9}$ ) as $a_{1}=a_{2}a_{3}a_{2}^{-1}$ , $b_{1}=a_{2}b_{3}a_{2}^{-1}$ to see that $[a_{1},b_{1}]=1$ . The surface relation in $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ then collapses to $[a_{2},b_{2}]=1$ . In summary, we have the following relations coming from the vanishing cycles $d_{7},\dots,d_{12}$ and the surface relation:

$$ a_{1}=a_{2}a_{3}a_{2}^{-1},\;b_{1}=a_{2}b_{3}a_{2}^{-1},\;[a_{3},b_{3}]=[b_{2},a_{3}]=[b_{2},b_{3}]=[a_{2},b_{2}]=1. $$

With some simplifications from (6), the vanishing cycles $B_{0},\dots,A_{2}$ contribute these relations (see also [6], equations (48)-(53)):

$$ a_{1}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

Note that the relations coming from $A_{0},A_{1},A_{2}$ are redundant, and that relation ( $B_{1}$ ) follows from ( $B_{0}$ ), ( $B_{2}$ ), and the fact that $[a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ .

Fix some $C=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&s\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ . Since $a_{1}$ and $b_{1}$ commute, we can let $\phi\in\Mod(\Sigma_{3}^{4})$ be an appropriate product of $t_{a_{1}}$ ’s and $t_{b_{1}}$ ’s so that $\phi(a_{1})=a_{1}^{p}b_{1}^{r}$ , $\phi(b_{1})=a_{1}^{q}b_{1}^{s}$ , and $\phi$ fixes the other standard generators of $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ . Hence the only two new relations coming from $\phi(B_{0}),\dots,\phi(A_{2})$ are:

$$ a_{1}^{p}b_{1}^{r}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ (a_{1}^{q}b_{1}^{s})^{-1}b_{2}b_{3}^{-1}=1 $$

In summary, $\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})$ is the group generated by $a_{1},b_{1},a_{2},b_{2},a_{3},b_{3}$ with relations (6), ( $\phi(B_{0})$ ), and ( $\phi(B_{2})$ ). Using the first two relations in (6) to eliminate $a_{3}$ and $b_{3}$ , we get the following presentation of $\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})$ :

$$ \pi_{1}(X_{\phi})\cong\langle a_{1},b_{1},a_{2},b_{2}|a_{2}^{-1}a_{1}a_{2}=a_{1}^{-p}b_{1}^{-r},a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{2}=a_{1}^{-q}b_{1}^{-s}b_{2},\\
[a_{1},b_{1}]=[a_{1},b_{2}]=[b_{1},b_{2}]=[a_{2},b_{2}]=1\rangle. $$

It is clear from this presentation that $\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}$ , with $\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ generated by $\{a_{1},b_{1},b_{2}\}$ , $\mathbf{Z}$ generated by $a_{2}$ , and the action of $a_{2}$ on $\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ given by

$$ A=\begin{pmatrix}-p&-q&0\\
-r&-s&0\\
0&1&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

By computations identical to those in [6], Section 5.1, we find that $e(X_{\phi})=\sigma(X_{\phi})=0$ , so $c_{1}^{2}(X_{\phi})=0$ . By our identifications of $\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})$ with those of torus bundles below, we have that $b_{1}(X_{\phi})\geq 2$ . Hence Remark 2.2 applies and we can use Corollary 2.1 to determine the homeomorphism type of $X_{\phi}$ .

It is straightforward, although a bit tedious, to do a change of basis that makes $A$ look standard as in Proposition 3.1.

Suppose first that $p=-1$ and $r=0$ . Since $C\in\SL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ , we see that $s=-1$ and $C=\begin{pmatrix}-1&q\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ . Thus

$$ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-q&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&1&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

Set

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\
0&0&1\\
1&0&q\end{pmatrix}\in\GL(3,\mathbf{Z}). $$

Then

$$ PAP^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\
1&1&0\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, $$

so by Proposition 3.1 and Lemma 3.1, $X_{\phi}$ is homeomorphic to $M(T,I;0,0)$ for $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}$ . Note that this torus bundle is independent of $q$ and has a section.

Now suppose that $(p+1,r)\neq(0,0)$ . Let $d=\gcd(r,p+1)$ , and let $x,y\in\mathbf{Z}$ be such that $x\frac{p+1}{d}+y\frac{r}{d}=1$ . Set

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}x&y&0\\
0&0&1\\
-\frac{r}{d}&\frac{p+1}{d}&\frac{p+s+2}{d}\end{pmatrix}\in\GL(3,\mathbf{Z}). $$

Then

$$ P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{p+1}{d}&y\frac{p+s+2}{d}&-y\\
\frac{r}{d}&-x\frac{p+s+2}{d}&x\\
0&1&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

and hence

$$ PAP^{-1}=\\
\begin{pmatrix}\frac{p+1}{d}(x-d)-\frac{r}{d}(qx+sy)&\frac{p+s+2}{d}[y(x-d)+x(qx+sy)]&-y(x-d)-x(qx+sy)\\
\frac{r}{d}&1-x\frac{p+s+2}{d}&x\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

This shows, using Proposition 3.1 and Lemma 3.1, that $X_{\phi}$ is homeomorphic to $M(T,I;m,n)$ , where

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{p+1}{d}(x-d)-\frac{r}{d}(qx+sy)&\frac{p+s+2}{d}[y(x-d)+x(qx+sy)]\\
\frac{r}{d}&1-x\frac{p+s+2}{d}\end{pmatrix} $$

and $(m,n)=(y(x-d)+x(qx+sy),d-x)$ .

Observe that Proposition 1.2 implies that $M(T,I;m,n)$ has a section if and only if $\binom{m}{n}$ is in the $\mathbf{Z}$ -span of the columns of $T-I$ . We have that

$$ \begin{split}(p+1)(x-d)-r(qx+sy)-d&=x(p+1-rq)-rsy-d(p+1)-d\\
&=x(p+1-rq)-rsy-d(p+2)\\
&=x(p+1+1-ps)-rsy-d(p+2)\\
&=x(p+2)-xps-rsy-d(p+2)\\
&=(x-d)(p+2)-s(xp+ry)\\
&=(x-d)(p+2)-s(d-x)\\
&=(x-d)(p+s+2),\end{split} $$

which shows that the columns of $T-I$ are

$$ v=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{p+s+2}{d}(x-d)\\
\frac{r}{d}\end{pmatrix},w=\frac{p+s+2}{d}\begin{pmatrix}y(x-d)+x(qx+sy)\\
-x\end{pmatrix}. $$

Write $v_{1}=\frac{p+s+2}{d}(x-d)$ and $w_{1}=y(x-d)+x(qx+sy)$ for convenience, so

$$ v=\begin{pmatrix}v_{1}\\
\frac{r}{d}\end{pmatrix},w=\frac{p+s+2}{d}\begin{pmatrix}w_{1}\\
-x\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}m\\
n\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}w_{1}\\
d-x\end{pmatrix}. $$

Note that

$$ \begin{split}rw_{1}&=ry(x-d)+rx(qx+sy)\\
&=(x-d)(d-x(p+1))+rqx^{2}+xs(d-x(p+1))\\
&=-d^{2}+d(x(p+1)+x)-x^{2}(p+1)+rqx^{2}+dsx-x^{2}s(p+1)\\
&=-d^{2}+dx(p+2+s)-x^{2}(p+1-rq+sp+s)\\
&=-d^{2}+dx(p+s+2)-x^{2}(p+s+2)\\
&=-d^{2}-x(x-d)(p+s+2).\end{split} $$

Since $\det(T-\lambda I)=\lambda^{2}-(\text{tr }T)\lambda+1$ , we see that

$$ \det(T-I)=2-\text{tr }T=-\text{tr}(T-I)=p+s+2. $$

If $p+s+2\neq 0$ , then $\binom{m}{n}$ is of course in the $\mathbf{Q}$ -span of $v,w$ : writing $av+bw=\binom{m}{n}$ , we see that

$$ \begin{split}a&=\frac{1}{p+s+2}(w_{1}(-x\frac{p+s+2}{d})-(d-x)(\frac{p+s+2}{d}w_{1}))\\
&=-\frac{w_{1}x}{d}-\frac{w_{1}(d-x)}{d}=-w_{1}\in\mathbf{Z}\\
b&=\frac{1}{p+s+2}(-\frac{r}{d}w_{1}+\frac{p+s+2}{d}(x-d)(d-x))\\
&=\frac{1}{d(p+s+2)}(-rw_{1}-(p+s+2)(x-d)^{2})\\
&=\frac{1}{d(p+s+2)}(d^{2}+x(x-d)(p+s+2)-(x-d)^{2}(p+s+2))\\
&=\frac{1}{d(p+s+2)}(d^{2}+d(x-d)(p+s+2))\\
&=x-d+\frac{d}{p+s+2},\end{split} $$

so $a,b\in\mathbf{Z}$ if and only if $p+s+2$ divides $d$ .

If $p+s+2=0$ , then

$$ v=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\frac{r}{d}\end{pmatrix},w=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\end{pmatrix}, $$

and (8) implies $rz_{1}=-d^{2}\neq 0$ , so $z_{1}\neq 0$ , and thus $\binom{m}{n}=\binom{z_{1}}{d-x}$ is not in the $\mathbf{Z}$ -span of $v,w$ .

To summarize, we have shown:

#### Theorem 5.1.

Let $C=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&s\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ and suppose $(p,r)\neq(-1,0)$ . Let $d=\gcd(r,p+1)$ , and let $x,y\in\mathbf{Z}$ be such that $x(p+1)+yr=d$ . Then there is a genus-3 Lefschetz pencil with total space homeomorphic to $M(T,I;m,n)$ , with

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{p+1}{d}(x-d)-\frac{r}{d}(qx+sy)&\frac{p+s+2}{d}[y(x-d)+x(qx+sy)]\\
\frac{r}{d}&1-x\frac{p+s+2}{d}\end{pmatrix} $$

and $(m,n)=(y(x-d)+x(qx+sy),d-x)$ . This torus bundle has a section if and only if $p+s+2$ is nonzero and divides $d$ .

#### Remark 5.2.

The case where $(p,r)=(-1,0)$ produced a torus bundle with a section, which is not new since Hamada-Hayano [3] constructed, for any commuting pair $A,B\in\SL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ , a genus-3 Lefschetz pencil with total space homeomorphic to $M(A,B;0,0)$ .

## 6. Genus-3 pencils from genus-2 relations of type $(4,3)$

The previous pencils were obtained by breeding two copies of a genus-2 relation of type $(6,2)$ . It is also possible to obtain genus-3 SCY pencils by breeding relations of type $(4,3)$ . We compute some examples in this section, although it is not clear how to systematically carry out the fundamental group computations like we did in the previous section.

Our first example uses Hamada’s (4,3) relation (see [9], Theorem 3), which was originally written down as a genus-2 Lefschetz fibration but has a lift to $\Mod(\Sigma_{2}^{3})$ , giving a genus-2 pencil with 3 basepoints [4]:

$$ t_{\sigma}t_{E}t_{\gamma}t_{F}t_{G}t_{\alpha}t_{D}=t_{d_{1}}t_{d_{2}}t_{d_{3}}. $$

See Figure 1 for the vanishing cycles.

Under these embeddings, the relation (9) becomes

$$ t_{C}t_{E}t_{\gamma}t_{F}t_{G}t_{\alpha}t_{D}=t_{C^{\prime}}t_{\delta_{4}}t_{\delta_{2}}, $$

For any mapping class $\phi\in\Mod(\Sigma_{3}^{4})$ that fixes $C^{\prime}$ and $C$ , we may conjugate (10) by $\phi$ to obtain

$$ t_{C}t_{\phi(E)}t_{\phi(\gamma)}t_{\phi(F)}t_{\phi(G)}t_{\phi(\alpha)}t_{\phi(D)}=t_{C^{\prime}}t_{\delta_{4}}t_{\delta_{2}}. $$

Moving $t_{C}$ to the right in the above equation, and moving $t_{C^{\prime}}$ to the right in (11), we may breed to obtain the following genus-3 Lefschetz pencil with 4-basepoints.

$$ t_{E^{\prime}}t_{\gamma^{\prime}}t_{F^{\prime}}t_{G^{\prime}}t_{\alpha^{\prime}}t_{D^{\prime}}t_{\phi(E)}t_{\phi(\gamma)}t_{\phi(F)}t_{\phi(G)}t_{\phi(\alpha)}t_{\phi(D)}=t_{\delta_{1}}t_{\delta_{2}}t_{\delta_{3}}t_{\delta_{4}} $$

Note that the total space of the Lefschetz pencil has $e=\sigma=0$ , and hence $c_{1}^{2}=0$ . So Remark 2.2 applies.

#### Proposition 6.1.

Let $\phi=t_{b_{2}}^{k}$ in the pencil (12), and denote the total space by $X_{k}$ .

- (1) If $k=2t$ is even then $X_{k}$ is homeomorphic to $M(T,I;1,0)$ , where

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-t\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

- (2) If $k=2t+1$ is odd then $X_{k}$ is homeomorphic to $M(T,I;-t,1)$ , where

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-k\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

None of these torus bundles have sections.

#### Proof.

Writing the primed curves in terms of the standard basis for $\pi_{1}(\Sigma_{3})$ , we get the following relations in $\pi_{1}(X_{k})$ :

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}[b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}=1 $$

$$ [b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}b_{1}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}[a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

Using ( $D^{\prime}$ ), we see that $b_{1}^{-1}=[b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}$ . This allows us to simplify ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) and ( $G^{\prime}$ ) by getting rid of the commutators:

$$ a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{1}=1 $$

Using ( $E^{\prime}$ ) to replace $a_{2}b_{2}$ at the end of ( $F^{\prime}$ ), we get

$$ a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=1 $$

Relations ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) and ( $F^{\prime}$ ) both contain the word $a_{2}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}$ ; equating the rest of the relations ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) and ( $F^{\prime}$ ) gives

$$ b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}=b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{2}=a_{1}^{2}b_{1}^{-1} $$

so $a_{1}^{2},b_{1}$ commute. Replace ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) with this new relation, keeping the rest in their simplified form:

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}=b_{1}a_{1}^{2} $$

$$ [b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}=b_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}a_{2}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{2}b_{2}^{-1}a_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{1}=1 $$

In ( $G^{\prime}$ ), we can cancel the $b_{1}$ ’s since ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) tells us that $a_{1}^{2}$ and $b_{1}$ commute. Hence ( $G^{\prime}$ ) becomes $a_{2}=a_{1}^{-2}$ . Putting this in ( $E^{\prime}$ ), we see that

$$ a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{2}=1, $$

so $b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ . Now ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) implies that $a_{2}$ and $b_{2}$ commute, so we can cancel some terms in ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ) and ( $F^{\prime}$ ). Our relations have now simplified to:

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}=b_{1}a_{1}^{2} $$

$$ [b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}=b_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ a_{1}b_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}b_{2}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=1 $$

$$ a_{2}=a_{1}^{-2} $$

Using ( $E^{\prime}$ ) to substitute $b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ into ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ), we find that

$$ a_{1}(a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1})b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}(a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1})=1. $$

Cancelling the first and last $a_{1}$ ’s and using ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ) to see that $a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ , we get

$$ a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=1 $$

Using ( $E^{\prime}$ ) in ( $F^{\prime}$ ), we see that

$$ a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=1, $$

which is the same as ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ). This lets us eliminate ( $F^{\prime}$ ) from the relations. Note that ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ) is saying that $a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ and $b_{1}$ commute. At this point, we throw in the surface relation $[a_{1},b_{1}][a_{2},b_{2}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ , which simplifies to $[a_{1},b_{1}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ since $a_{2},b_{2}$ commute. Our relations are now

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}=b_{1}a_{1}^{2} $$

$$ [b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}=b_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ [a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1},b_{1}]=1 $$

$$ a_{2}=a_{1}^{-2} $$

$$ [a_{1},b_{1}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1 $$

Let us simplify ( $D^{\prime}$ ): using ( $E^{\prime}$ ) to substitute $b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}$ and ( $\Sigma$ ) to substitute $[b_{3},a_{3}]=[a_{1},b_{1}]$ gives

$$ a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}=b_{1}^{-1}, $$

which is the same as ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ). Hence we can eliminate ( $D^{\prime}$ ). In summary, the relations coming from the primed curves and the surface relation are:

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}=b_{1}a_{1}^{2},\;b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1},\;[a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1},b_{1}]=1, $$

$$ a_{2}=a_{1}^{-2},\;[a_{1},b_{1}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1. $$

We now analyze the relations coming from the unprimed curves in (12), with $\phi=t_{b_{2}}^{k}$ :

$$ a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{3}b_{2}=1 $$

$$ [b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}a_{2}b_{2}^{-k}a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}[a_{3},b_{3}]a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}[b_{3},a_{3}]b_{2}a_{2}b_{2}^{-k}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-k}b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}=1 $$

Using ( $\phi(D)$ ) to get rid of the $b_{2}b_{3}$ term in ( $\phi(\alpha)$ ), we see that $a_{3}^{2}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-2}b_{3}=1$ , so that $a_{3}^{2}$ and $b_{3}$ commute. Substituting $b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}$ , ( $\phi(D)$ ) becomes $b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ . Using ( $\phi(D)$ ) in ( $\phi(F)$ ) to replace $b_{2}^{-1}$ with $b_{3}$ produces ( $\phi(E)$ ), so we can eliminate ( $\phi(E)$ ). We use the relation ( $D^{\prime}$ ) from the primed curves to get rid of commutators in the remaining relations:

$$ a_{3}^{2}b_{3}=b_{3}a_{3}^{2} $$

$$ b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{2}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{1}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-k}a_{3}=1 $$

$$ a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{2}b_{2}^{-k-1}a_{3}=1 $$

The relation ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ) implies that $b_{2}^{-1}a_{3}b_{1}^{-1}=a_{3}$ , and putting this into ( $\phi(F)$ ) gives $a_{3}a_{2}b_{2}^{-k}a_{3}=1$ . Expressing $a_{2}$ and $b_{2}$ in terms of $a_{1},b_{1}$ gives

$$ a_{3}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{k}a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}=1. $$

Substituting $b_{2}=a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}$ into ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ) gives $b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}=1$ , and this becomes $b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}=1$ after using ( $\phi(D)$ ). In other words, ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ) has become $b_{3}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}$ .

Expressing $a_{2}$ and $b_{2}$ in terms of $a_{1},b_{1}$ in ( $\phi(G)$ ) gives

$$ a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{k+1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}=1. $$

By ( $\phi(F)$ ), we have $b_{1}^{k}a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}=a_{1}a_{3}^{-1}$ , so substituting this above gives $a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}a_{3}^{-1}=1$ . Cancelling the $a_{3}$ ’s gives $b_{3}=a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}$ , and since $a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ by ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ), we get $b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ . This is precisely ( $\phi(D)$ ), so we can get rid of ( $\phi(G)$ ) from our relations.

Let us write ( $\phi(F)$ ) slightly differently: the relations $b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ and $b_{3}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}$ imply that $b_{1}$ commutes with $a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}$ , so we can commute $b_{1}^{k}$ all the way to the right in ( $\phi(F)$ ):

$$ a_{3}a_{1}^{-2}a_{3}=b_{1}^{-k} $$

Summarizing, the relations from the unprimed curves collapse to:

$$ a_{3}^{2}b_{3}=b_{3}a_{3}^{2} $$

$$ b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{3}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1} $$

$$ a_{3}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{k}a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}=1 $$

Observe that the surface relation $[a_{1},b_{1}][a_{3},b_{3}]=1$ is equivalent to $a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}^{-1}=b_{3}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}$ , and using ( $\phi(D)$ ) gives $b_{3}b_{1}^{-1}=b_{3}a_{3}b_{3}^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}$ . Cancelling the leftmost $b_{3}$ ’s gives a relation equivalent to ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ), so we can eliminate the surface relation.

We are done simplifying the relations; the remaining relations are ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ), ( $E^{\prime}$ ), ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ), ( $G^{\prime}$ ), ( $\phi(\alpha)$ ), ( $\phi(D)$ ), ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ), and ( $\phi(F)$ ). The relations ( $E^{\prime}$ ) and ( $G^{\prime}$ ) eliminate the generators $a_{2},b_{2}$ , so we are left with the following presentation of $\pi_{1}(X_{k})$ :

$$ \pi_{1}(X_{k})\cong\langle a_{1},b_{1},a_{3},b_{3}|(\alpha^{\prime}),(\gamma^{\prime}),(\phi(\alpha)),(\phi(D)),(\phi(\gamma)),(\phi(F))\rangle, $$

with

$$ a_{1}^{2}b_{1}=b_{1}a_{1}^{2} $$

$$ [a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1},b_{1}]=1 $$

$$ a_{3}^{2}b_{3}=b_{3}a_{3}^{2} $$

$$ b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1} $$

$$ b_{3}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1} $$

$$ a_{3}a_{1}^{-2}a_{3}=b_{1}^{-k} $$

It is not immediately clear from this presentation whether $\pi_{1}(X_{k})$ is the of the form in Proposition 1.1, so we make a change-of-basis. Replace the generator $a_{1}$ by

$$ c=a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}, $$

so that $c,b_{1},a_{3},b_{3}$ is our new generating set for $\pi_{1}(X_{k})$ .

Using the relations between $a_{1},b_{1},a_{3}$ , and $b_{3}$ , we observe the following relations between $c,b_{1},a_{3}$ , and $b_{3}$ :

$$ \begin{split}cb_{1}c^{-1}&=a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}\\
&=a_{3}^{-1}b_{3}a_{3}\\
&=b_{1}\end{split} $$

$$ \begin{split}c^{-1}b_{3}c&=a_{1}^{-1}a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}\\
&=a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}\\
&=b_{3}\end{split} $$

$$ b_{1}^{-k}=a_{3}(a_{3}c)^{-2}a_{3}=a_{3}c^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}c^{-1} $$

$$ a_{3}c^{-1}a_{3}^{-1}=b_{1}^{-k}c $$

$$ a_{3}ca_{3}^{-1}=c^{-1}b_{1}^{k} $$

$$ [b_{1},b_{3}]=[b_{1},a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}]=1 $$

$$ a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}=a_{3}^{2}b_{1}a_{3}^{-2}=b_{1} $$

$$ b_{3}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1} $$

Conversely, suppose we are only given the relations (13), (14), (15), (16), (17), and ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ). We will derive the relations ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ), ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ), ( $\phi(\alpha)$ ), ( $\phi(D)$ ), and ( $\phi(F)$ ):

- $\phi(\alpha)$ : Starting with ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ) and using (17), we get

$$ b_{3}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}=a_{3}^{2}b_{3}a_{3}^{-2}, $$

which is ( $\phi(\alpha)$ ).

- $\phi(D)$ : Using $c=a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ in (13), we get $a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}b_{1}=b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ , and thus $a_{1}b_{1}=a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ . Using ( $\phi(\gamma)$ ) then gives $a_{1}b_{1}=b_{3}a_{1}$ , which is ( $\phi(D)$ ).

- $\alpha^{\prime}$ : Using $c=a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ in (14), we get $a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}b_{3}=b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ , and hence $a_{1}b_{3}=a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ . Now use (17) to get $a_{1}b_{3}=b_{1}a_{1}$ . Thus $b_{3}=a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}$ . We derived ( $\phi(D)$ ) above, which says that $b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ . We see that $a_{1}^{-1}b_{1}a_{1}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ , which is equivalent to ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ ).

- $\gamma^{\prime}$ : We derived above that $b_{3}=a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}$ . Hence the relation (16) becomes $[b_{1},a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1}]=1$ , which is ( $\gamma^{\prime}$ ).

- $\phi(F)$ : In the process of deriving (15) from ( $\phi(F)$ ), we only used $c=a_{3}^{-1}a_{1}$ ; no other relations were used. Hence (15) and ( $\phi(F)$ ) are equivalent.

Hence under the two sets of generators $a_{1},b_{1},a_{3},b_{3}$ and $c=a_{3}^{-1}a_{1},b_{1},a_{3},b_{3}$ , the sets of relations ( $\alpha^{\prime}$ )-( $\phi(F)$ ) and (13)-( $\phi(\gamma)$ ) are equivalent. So

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{1}(X_{k})\cong\langle c,b_{1},a_{3},b_{3}|[c,b_{1}]=[c,b_{3}]=[b_{1},b_{3}]=1, \displaystyle a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1}=b_{1},a_{3}b_{1}a_{3}^{-1}=b_{3},a_{3}ca_{3}^{-1}=c^{-1}b_{1}^{k}\rangle $$

From this presentation, it is clear that $\pi_{1}(X_{k})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{3}\rtimes_{A}\mathbf{Z}$ , with $\mathbf{Z}^{3}$ generated by $\{b_{1},b_{3},c\}$ , $\mathbf{Z}$ generated by $a_{3}$ , and

$$ A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&k\\
1&0&0\\
0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

If $k=2t$ is even, take

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\
0&0&1\\
1&1&t\end{pmatrix}, $$

so that

$$ PAP^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-t&1\\
0&-1&0\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

By Lemma 3.1 and Proposotion 3.1, $X_{k}\cong M(T,I;1,0)$ , where

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-t\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

By Proposition 1.2, this torus bundle does not have a section.

If $k=2t+1$ is odd, take

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&t\\
1&1&t\\
2&2&2t+1\end{pmatrix}, $$

so that

$$ PAP^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-k&t+1\\
0&-1&1\\
0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

By Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.1, $X_{k}\cong M(T,I;-t,1)$ , where

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-k\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

By Proposition 1.2, this torus bundle does not have a section. ∎

#### Remark 6.1.

The relations coming from the primed curves imply that $a_{2}$ and $b_{2}$ commute. Thus, given any $\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ r&s\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbf{Z})$ we can let $\phi$ be an appropriate product of $t_{a_{2}}$ ’s and $t_{b_{2}}$ ’s so that $\phi(a_{2})=a_{2}^{p}b_{2}^{r}$ , $\phi(b_{2})=a_{2}^{q}b_{2}^{s}$ , and $\phi$ fixes the other generators. It is then not too difficult to determine the relations coming from the unprimed curves, now conjugated by $\phi$ . When combined with the relations coming from the primed curves we get the following presentation for $\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})$ , where $X_{\phi}$ is the total space of the pencil (12):

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})\cong\langle a_{1},b_{1},a_{3},b_{3}|b_{3}=a_{1}^{2q+1}b_{1}^{s}a_{1}^{-1},a_{3}^{2}=a_{1}^{2p+1}b_{1}^{r}a_{1}^{-1}, \displaystyle[a_{1}^{2},b_{1}]=[a_{1}b_{1}a_{1}^{-1},b_{1}]=[a_{1},b_{1}][a_{3},b_{3}]=[a_{3}b_{3}a_{3}^{-1},b_{3}]=1\rangle. $$

It is not clear to the author how to recognize this as the fundamental group of a torus bundle.

#### Remark 6.2.

Taking $\phi$ to be $t_{b_{3}}$ , $t_{b_{3}}t_{a_{3}}$ , $t_{a_{3}}t_{b_{3}}t_{a_{3}}$ , or $t_{a_{3}}t_{b_{3}}^{-1}t_{a_{3}}$ will all result in a fundamental group isomorphic to $\pi_{1}(M(-I,I;0,-1))$ . It is possible, but tedious, to do these computations by hand, and we do not include them here because they are similar to our previous computations. Alternatively, one can put the original group presentations for $\pi_{1}(X_{\phi})$ and $\pi_{1}(M(-I,I;0,-1))$ into a computer algebra system and see that they both simplify to the same finitely-presented group.

# On $\chi$ -slice pretzel links

**Authors:** Sophia Fanelle , Evan Huang , Ben Huenemann , Weizhe Shen , Jonathan Simone and Hannah Turner

## Abstract

A link is called $\chi-$ slice if it bounds a smooth properly embedded surface in the 4-ball with no closed components and Euler characteristic 1. If a link has a single component, then it is $\chi-$ slice if and only if it is slice. One motivation for studying such links is that the double cover of the 3-sphere branched along a nonzero determinant $\chi-$ slice link is a rational homology 3-sphere that bounds a rational homology 4-ball. This article aims to generalize known results about the sliceness of pretzel knots to the $\chi-$ sliceness of pretzel links. In particular, we completely classify positive and negative pretzel links that are $\chi-$ slice, and obtain partial classifications of 3-stranded and 4-stranded pretzel links that are $\chi-$ slice. As a consequence, we obtain infinite families of Seifert fiber spaces that bound rational homology 4-balls.

## 1. Introduction

A knot in $S^{3}$ is called slice if it bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^{4}$ . One motivation behind studying slice knots is that the double cover of $S^{3}$ branched along a slice knot is a rational homology 3-sphere that bounds a rational homology 4-ball. The question of which rational homology 3-spheres bound rational homology 4-balls is a well-known open problem in low-dimensional topology.

There are two generalizations of sliceness to links—the classical notion of slice links and the more recently defined notion of $\chi-$ slice links [3]. A link $L\subset S^{3}$ is $\chi$ -slice if it bounds an embedded surface in $B^{4}$ with no closed components and Euler characteristic $\chi=1$ . We call a smooth properly embedded Euler characteristic 1 surface in $B^{4}$ without closed components whose boundary is $L$ a $\chi-$ slice surface for $L$ . Moreover, if $F$ is a $\chi-$ slice surface for $L$ and $F$ can be smoothly isotoped rel boundary so that the radial distance function restricted to $F$ has no local maxima, then $L$ is called $\chi-$ ribbon and $F$ is called a $\chi-$ ribbon surface. Figure 1 shows an example of a $\chi-$ ribbon link $L$ along with a $\chi-$ ribbon surface for $L$ . Note that a knot is $\chi-$ slice (resp. $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if it is slice (resp. ribbon). This generalization of sliceness to links is natural from the 4-manifold perspective as the following result shows.

*Figure 1. An example of a $\chi-$ slice surface $F$ bounded by the link $T(2,4)$ . $F$ is the union of a disk and a Mobius band.*

#### Proposition 1.1 (Proposition 2.6 in [3]).

If $L$ is a $\chi-$ slice link with det $L\neq 0$ , then the double cover of $S^{3}$ branched along $L$ is a rational homology 3-sphere that bounds a rational homology 4-ball.

Generically, an infinite family of nonzero determinant $\chi-$ slice links, gives rise to an infinite family of rational homology 3-spheres bounding rational homology 4-balls.

#### Remark 1.2.

Recall that an $n$ component link $L\subset S^{3}$ is slice if $L$ bounds the disjoint union of $n$ smooth properly embedded disks in $B^{4}$ . It is known that if a link $L$ is slice, then $\det L=0$ ; consequently the double cover of $S^{3}$ branched along $L$ is not a rational homology 3-sphere. Hence the notions of nonzero determinant $\chi-$ slice links and slice links (with more than 1 component) are disjoint.

In this paper, we will explore the $\chi$ -sliceness of pretzel links with the aim of extending known results regarding the the sliceness of pretzel knots in [6], [11], [13], and [8]. We first use ribbon moves to construct infinite families of $\chi-$ slice pretzel links. Then, to obstruct other pretzel links from being $\chi-$ slice, we use Proposition 1.1 and expand on the sliceness obstructions developed in [6] stemming from Donaldson’s Diagonalization Theorem and Heegaard Floer correction terms; moreover, we apply several geometric obstructions specific to links of multiple components.

The $m$ -stranded pretzel link $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ is the link depicted in Figure 2, where the boxes labeled $p_{i}$ indicate $p_{i}$ half-twists. We will focus on three classes of pretzel links: positive (and negative) pretzel links, 3-stranded pretzel links, and 4-stranded pretzel links. Note that $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ is isotopic to $P(p_{m},\ldots,p_{1})$ and if $(p_{i_{1}},\ldots,p_{i_{m}})$ is a cyclic reordering of $(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ , then $P(p_{i_{1}},\ldots,p_{i_{m}})$ is isotopic to $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ . We set:

$$ P\langle p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\rangle:=\{P(p_{i_{1}},\ldots,p_{i_{m}})\,:\,(p_{i_{1}},\ldots,p_{i_{m}})\text{ is any reordering of }(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})\} $$

We denote the mirror of a link $L$ by $-L$ . Note that $-P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})=P(-p_{1},\ldots,-p_{m})$ . For convenience, a sequence $(\dots,\overbrace{x,\ldots,x}^{t},\ldots)$ will be denoted by $(\dots,x^{[t]},\ldots)$ . Finally, we take the convention that a pretzel link

$P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ satisfies $m\geq 3$ and $p_{i}\neq 0$ for all $i$ .

*Figure 2. The $m-$ stranded pretzel link $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ , where the boxes labeled $p_{i}$ indicate $p_{i}$ half-twists and the 3-stranded pretzel knot $P(-3,3,-3)$ .*

### 1.1. Positive and negative pretzel links

A pretzel link $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ , where $m\geq 3$ , is called positive (resp. negative) if $p_{i}>0$ (resp. $p_{i}<0$ ) for all $1\leq i\leq m$ . Our first result classifies $\chi-$ slice positive pretzel links and $\chi-$ slice negative pretzel links. Note that since $P(-p_{1},\ldots,-p_{m})$ is simply the mirror of $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ , $P(-p_{1},\ldots,-p_{m})$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ is $\chi-$ slice.

#### Theorem 1.3.

A positive (resp. negative) pretzel link $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if $L$ (resp. $-L$ ) is isotopic to $P(2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2)$ or $P(1^{[z]},2^{[2k]},k+z\pm 2)$ , where $k,z\geq 0$ are integers satisfying $z+2k\geq 2$ and $k+z\pm 2\geq 1$ . Moreover, $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if L is $\chi-$ ribbon.

### 1.2. 3-stranded pretzel links

Note that a 3-stranded pretzel link $P(p,q,r)$ is a knot if and only if either all parameters are odd or exactly one of the parameters is even. Let

$$ \mathcal{E}=\left\{P\left(a,-(a+2),-\frac{(a+1)^{2}}{2}\right)\,:\,a\text{ is odd and }a\equiv 1,97\mod{120}\right\}. $$

We first summarize known results from the literature regarding the sliceness of 3-stranded pretzel knots.

#### Theorem 1.4 ([12],[6],[11],[13],[8]).

Assume that $K$ is a 3-stranded pretzel knot such that $K,-K\not\in\mathcal{E}$ . Then $K$ is slice if and only if $K$ or $-K$ is isotopic to one of the links in the following sets:

- • $\{P(1,1,4),P(1,-2,-3),P(1,-3,-6)\}$ ;

- • $\{P(1,a,-(a+4))\,|\,a\geq 1\text{ is odd}\}$ ; or

- • $\{P(a,-a,b)\,|\,a\geq 1\text{ is odd and }b\geq 1\}$ .

Moreover, $K$ is slice if and only if $K$ is ribbon.

#### Remark 1.5.

It is worth mentioning that there is evidence that every pretzel knot in $\mathcal{E}$ is not slice. In [11], Lecuona points out that if $a\leq 1597$ , then $P(a,-a-2,-\frac{(a+1)^{2}}{2})$ is not slice (checked via computer).

Our next result can be thought of as a generalization of Theorem 1.4 to the $\chi-$ sliceness of pretzel links. We first define a set that contains the set $\mathcal{E}$ . Let

$$ \mathcal{F}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{c c}\!\!\hbox{\multirowsetup$P(a,-a-x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2},-a-y_{1}^{2}-y_{2}^{2})\,\,:$ }&\!\!\Big|\!\det\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&y_{1}\\
x_{2}&y_{2}\end{bmatrix}\!\Big|\leq 4,\,\,\,x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}=-a,\\
&\text{and exactly two parameters are even}\end{array}\right\}\cup\mathcal{E}. $$

#### Theorem 1.6.

Suppose $L$ is 3-stranded pretzel link with nonzero determinant and $L,-L\not\in\mathcal{F}$ . Then $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if $L$ or $-L$ is isotopic to one of the links in the following sets:

- • $\{P(1,1,4),P(1,-2,-3),P(1,-3,-6),P(1,-2,-6),P(2,2,3),P(2,2,-5)\}$ ;

- • $\{P(1,a,-(a+4))\,|\,a\geq 1\}$ ; or

- • $\{P(a,-a,b)\,|\,a,b\geq 1\}$ .

Moreover, $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if $L$ is $\chi-$ ribbon.

#### Remark 1.7.

If $K\in\mathcal{E}$ , then $K$ is isotopic to a knot whose parameters are given by the formula in the first set comprising $\mathcal{F}$ . In particular, if $a=120k+b$ , where $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $b\in\{1,97\}$ , then $x_{1}=x_{2}=-1$ , $y_{1}=60k+b$ , and $y_{2}=60k$ . It is worth noting that the obstruction used to obtain the set $\mathcal{F}$ obtains the same formula in the case of $P(p,q,r)$ having exactly one even parameter. However, this list of potentially slice pretzel knots is reduced further in [11],[13], and [8] by using Casson-Gordon invariants and the Fox-Milnor condition. These computations could potentially be carried out in the case when there are two even parameters, however they would only help in obstructing the existence of orientable $\chi-$ slice surfaces ([3], [5]).

### 1.3. 4-stranded pretzel links

We recall the following result regarding the sliceness of 4-stranded pretzel knots due to Lecuona.

#### Theorem 1.8 ([11]).

Suppose $K$ is a 4-stranded pretzel link. If $K$ is slice, then there exist odd integers $a,b\geq 1$ such that $K$ or $-K$ is isotopic to a link in the set $P\langle a,-(a+1),b,-b\rangle.$ Moreover, if $K$ or $-K$ is isotopic to $P(a,-(a+1),b,-b)$ for some odd integers $a,b\geq 1$ , then $K$ is $\chi-$ ribbon.

#### Remark 1.9.

It unknown in general whether the 4-stranded pretzel knots of the form $P(a,b,-(a+1),-b)$ , where $a$ and $b$ are odd, are slice.

We are able to extend this result by determining many infinite families that are $\chi-$ slice and obstruct “most” remaining 4-stranded pretzel links from being $\chi-$ slice.

#### Theorem 1.10.

Let $a\geq 1$ and $b\neq 0$ . The following 4-stranded pretzel links (and their mirrors) are $\chi-$ ribbon:

- • $P(1,1,1,1),P(1,1,1,5),P(2,2,-3,-6),P(1,1,-2,-6)$ ,

- • $P(a,2,2,-1),P(a,2,2,-a),P(a,2,2,-(a+4))$ ,

- • $P(a,3,1,-a),P(a,3,1,-(a+3)),P(a,1,-2,-2)$ ,

- • $P(a,b,-b,-(a+1))$ , and $P(a,b,-b,-(a+4)).$

#### Theorem 1.11.

If a 4-stranded pretzel link $L$ with nonzero determinant is $\chi$ -slice, then $L$ or $-L$ is isotopic to one of the pretzel links listed in Theorem 1.10 or to one of the pretzel links in the following sets (where $a,b\geq 1$ ):

- • $\{P(2,a,2,-a),P(2,a,2,-(a+4)),P(a,b,-(a+1),-b),P(a,b,-(a+4),-b)\}$ ;

- • $\{P\langle a,b,-b-x^{2},-b-y^{2}\rangle\,:\,xy=-b\text{ and }a\geq\frac{(|x|+|y|-2)b-2}{2}\}$ ; or

- • $\{P\langle a,-a-x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2}-x_{3}^{2},-a-y_{1}^{2}-y_{2}^{2}-x_{3}^{2},-a-z_{1}^{2}-z_{2}^{2}-z_{3}^{2}\rangle\},$ where

$$ \Big|\det\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&y_{1}&z_{1}\\ x_{2}&y_{2}&z_{2}\\ x_{3}&y_{3}&z_{3}\end{bmatrix}\Big|\leq 8 $$

and $x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3}=x_{1}z_{1}+x_{2}z_{2}+x_{3}z_{3}=y_{1}z_{1}+y_{2}z_{2}+y_{3}z_{3}=-a.$

Note that many of the $\chi-$ slice pretzel links in Theorem 1.10 have the same (unordered) parameters as the potentially $\chi-$ slice pretzel links given in the first bullet of Theorem 1.11 (e.g. $P(a,2,2,-a)$ compared to $P(2,a,2,-a)$ ). This is due to the obstructions used in the proof of Theorem 1.11—Donaldson’s Diagonalization Theorem [4], lattice embeddings, and Heegaard Floer $d-$ invariant calculations. Our proof strategy largely follows the strategy employed in [6], but adapted to the case of links. In general, these obstructions cannot differentiate between different orderings of the parameters. We are able to differentiate between some of the orderings (e.g. we are able to show that $P(2,-3,2,-6)$ is not $\chi-$ slice even though $P(2,2,-3,-6)$ is $\chi-$ slice) using geometric arguments (see Section 3.1).

#### Remark 1.12.

There are knot invariant obstructions that can tell the difference between different orderings of the parameters, but these would only obstruct the existence of orientable $\chi-$ slice surfaces. For example, in [3], it is shown that if the signature of a link is nonzero, then it cannot bound an orientable $\chi-$ slice surface; and in [5], it is shown that if the Alexander polynomial of an oriented link satisfies the Fox-Milnor condition, then it cannot bound an orientable $\chi-$ slice surface.

### 1.4. Seifert fiber spaces bounding rational homology 4-balls

Following as in [11], let $Y(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ denote the double cover of $S^{3}$ branched over the pretzel link $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ . This 3-manifold can be realized as the boundary of the 4-dimensional plumbing shown in Figure 3. In particular, $Y(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$ is a Seifert fiber space. The next result follows from Proposition 1.1 and Theorems 1.3, 1.6, and 1.10; it provides infinite families of Seifert fiber spaces bounding rational homology 4-balls, some of which are known in the literature (see, e.g., [11], [9]).

*Figure 3. The double cover of $S^{3}$ branched along $P(p_{1},\ldots,p_{m})$*

#### Theorem 1.13.

The following Seifert fiber spaces bound rational homology 4-balls.

- • $Y(1,1,4),Y(1,-2,-3),Y(1,-3,-6),Y(1,-2,-6),Y(2,2,3),Y(2,2,-5)$

- • $Y(1,a,-(a+4))$ , where $a\geq 1$

- • $Y(a,-a,b)$ , where $a,b\geq 1$

- • $Y(1,1,1,1),Y(1,1,1,5),Y(2,2,-3,-6),Y(1,1,-2,-6)$

- • $Y(a,2,2,-1),Y(a,2,2,-a),Y(a,2,2,-(a+4))$ , where $a\geq 1$

- • $Y(a,3,1,-a),Y(a,3,1,-(a+3)),Y(a,1,-2,-2)$ , where $a\geq 1$

- • $Y(a,b,-b,-(a+1)),Y(a,b,-b,-(a+4))$ , where $a\geq 1,\,b\neq 0$

- • $Y(2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2)$

- • $Y(1^{[z]},2^{[2k]},k+z\pm 2)$ , where $k,z\geq 0$ such that $z+2k\geq 2$ and $k+z\pm 2\geq 1$

### 1.5. Organization

In Section 2 we prove that certain pretzel links are $\chi-$ slice via ribbon moves, proving Theorem 1.10 and one direction of Theorems 1.3 and 1.6. In Section 3, we will recall important facts about pretzel links and provide overviews of the main obstructions used to finish the proofs of Theorems 1.3 and 1.6 and to prove Theorem 1.11. Section 4 contains the proof of Theorem 1.3, Section 5 contains the proof of Theorem 1.6, and Section 6 contains the proof of Theorem 1.11.

### 1.6. Acknowledgments

## 2. Ribbon Moves

In this section we show that several families of pretzel links are $\chi-$ ribbon (and hence $\chi-$ slice) by finding ribbon moves in their diagrams to explicitly describe a $\chi-$ ribbon surface for the the link. In particular we prove Theorem 1.10 and one direction of Theorem 1.6. We first review the classification of $\chi-$ slice 2-bridge links due to Lisca in [12], which will be used in the aforementioned proofs.

### 2.1. $\chi-$ slice 2-bridge links

In [12], Lisca classified $\chi-$ slice 2-bridge links (although the term “ $\chi-$ slice” was not coined until after Lisca’s findings). We will rely on this classification for proving the $\chi-$ sliceness of particular families of pretzel links.

For integers $x_{1},\ldots,x_{y}\neq 0$ , we define the following two continued fraction expansions:

$$ [x_{1},\ldots,x_{y}]^{+}=x_{1}+\frac{1}{\displaystyle x_{2}+\frac{1}{\displaystyle\cdots+\frac{1}{x_{y}}}}\,\,\,\,\text{ and }\,\,\,\,[x_{1},\ldots,x_{y}]^{-}=x_{1}-\frac{1}{\displaystyle x_{2}-\frac{1}{\displaystyle\cdots-\frac{1}{x_{y}}}}. $$

Up to mirroring, every 2-bridge link is isotopic to a link of the form $C(d_{1},\ldots,d_{m})$ shown in Figure 4, where $d_{i}\neq 0$ for all $i$ . Moreover, it is known that every 2-bridge link is isotopic to a link of the form $C(d_{1},\ldots,d_{m})$ with $d_{i}>0$ for all $i$ ; see e.g [7, Chapter 2]. Given a such 2-bridge link $C(d_{1},\ldots,d_{m})$ , we call the reduced fraction $\frac{p}{q}=[d_{1},\ldots,d_{m}]^{+}$ the classifying fraction of $C(d_{1},\ldots,d_{m})$ and denote $C(d_{1},\ldots,d_{m})$ with the simpler notation $K(p,q)$ . It follows that any 2-bridge link is isotopic to $K(p,q)$ for some $p>q>0$ . Finally, if $C(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k})$ (with $e_{i}\neq 0$ arbitrary) satisfies $[e_{1},\ldots,e_{k}]^{+}=\frac{p}{q}$ , then $C(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k})$ is isotopic to $K(p,q)$ .

*Figure 4. The two-bridge link $C(d_{1},\ldots,d_{m})$ is indicated in the case that $m$ is even (above) and when $m$ is odd (below).*

Given relatively prime integers $p>q>0$ , there exist unique integers $a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\geq 2$ such that $\frac{p}{q}=[a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}]^{-}$ . Let $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k})$ be an ordered string of integers such that $b_{i}\geq 2$ for all $i$ . If $b_{i}\geq 3$ for some $i$ , then we can write this string in the form

$$ (2^{[m_{1}]},3+n_{1},2^{[m_{2}]},3+n_{2},\ldots,2^{[m_{j-1}]},3+n_{j-1},2^{[m_{j}]},2+n_{j}), $$

where $m_{i},n_{i}\geq 0$ for all $i$ and $(\dots,x^{[t]},\ldots)$ denotes $(\dots,\overbrace{x,\ldots,x}^{t},\ldots)$ . The string $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{l})=(2+m_{1},2^{[n_{1}]},3+m_{2},2^{[n_{2}]},\ldots,3+m_{j-1},2^{[n_{j-1}]},3+m_{j},2^{[n_{j}]})$ is called the dual string of $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k})$ . If $b_{i}=2$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$ , then we define its dual string to be $(k+1)$ . Finally, we say $(c_{n},\ldots,c_{1})$ is the reverse of $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{n})$ .

#### Theorem 2.1 (Lemmas 7.1-7.3 in [12] and Remark 3.2 in [10]).

Let $\frac{p}{q}=[a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}]^{-}$ . $K(p,q)$ is $\chi-$ slice (and, indeed, $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if, up to reversal, $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})$ or its dual is of one of the following forms:

- (1) $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k},2,c_{l},\ldots,c_{1})$ , where $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k})$ and $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{l})$ are dual;

- (2) $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k-1},b_{k}+1,2,2,c_{l}+1,c_{l-1},\ldots,c_{1})$ , where $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k})$ and $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{l})$ are dual;

- (3) $(2^{[x]},3,2+y,2+x,3,2^{[y]})$ ;

- (4) $(2^{[x]},3+y,2,2+x,3,2^{[y]})$ ;

- (5) $(2+x,2+y,3,2^{[x]},4,2^{[y]})$ ;

- (6) $(2+x,2,3+y,2^{[x]},4,2^{[y]})$ ; or

- (7) $(3+x,2,3+y,3,2^{[x]},3,2^{[y]})$ .

#### Corollary 2.2.

The torus link $T(2,a)$ , where $a\neq 0$ , is $\chi-$ slice (and $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if $a\in\{\pm 1,\pm 4\}$ .

#### Proof.

The torus knots $T(2,1)$ and $T(2,-1)$ are isotopic to the unknot, so they are slice. Assume $a\neq\pm 1$ . The torus link $T(2,a)$ is isotopic to the 2-bridge link $C(a)$ . Suppose $a>1$ . Then $C(a)$ has classifying fraction $\frac{a}{1}=[a]^{-}$ . Notice that the string $(a)$ has dual $(2^{[a-1]}).$ The former string does not appear in the list of strings in Theorem 2.1. The latter string, however, is in the list of strings if and only if $a=4$ . Now since the mirror of $T(2,a)=C(a)$ is $T(2,-a)=C(-a)$ , the result follows. ∎

We now use the classification of $\chi-$ slice 2-bridge link to classify the $\chi-$ sliceness of particular 2-bridge pretzel links.

#### Lemma 2.3.

$P(1^{[z]},a)$ , where $a\geq 1$ , is $\chi-$ slice (and, indeed, $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if $a=z\pm 2$ , where $z\pm 2\geq 1$ .

#### Proof.

First note that a pretzel link of the form $P(1^{[z]},a)$ is the 2-bridge link $C(z,a)=K(az+1,a)$ . It is easy to verify that $[z+1,2^{[a-1]}]^{-}=\frac{az+1}{a}$ . Consider the list of strings in Theorem 2.1 and note that the dual of $(z+1,2^{[a-1]})$ is $(2^{[z-1]},a+1)$ . Since, up to reversal, these strings are not of the form $(b)-(g)$ , it follows that $(z+1,2^{[a-1]})$ or $(2^{[z-1]},a+1)$ is of type $(a)$ . The string $(z+1,2^{[a-1]})$ is of type $(a)$ if and only if $(z+1)$ and $(2^{[a-2]})$ are dual strings; that is, $z+2=a$ . On the other hand, $(2^{[z-1]},a+1)$ is of type $(a)$ if and only if $(2^{[z-2]})$ and $(a+1)$ are dual strings; that is, $z-2=a$ . ∎

The next result was noted (without proof) in Remark 1.3 in [6]. For completeness, we will prove it here.

#### Lemma 2.4.

Suppose $L$ is a 3-stranded pretzel link containing a parameter equal to 1 and with nonzero determinant. Then $L$ is $\chi-$ slice (and, indeed, $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if $L$ or $-L$ is isotopic to one of the links in the following sets:

- • $\{P(1,-3,-6),P(1,-2,-6),P(1,-2,-3),P(1,1,4)\}$

- • $\{P(1,-1,a)\,|\,a\geq 1\}$

- • $\{P(1,a,-a)\,|\,a\geq 1\}$

- • $\{P(1,a,-(a+4))\,|\,a\geq 1\}$

#### Proof.

Let $L=P(1,a,b)$ be a 3-stranded pretzel link with nonzero determinant. Note that if $a=-1$ or $b=-1$ , then $L$ is isotopic to $P(1,-1,a)$ , which is unknotted; this are the links in the second bullet point. If $a=1$ or $b=1$ , then $L$ is a twist knot. The only slice twist knots are the unknot and Stevedore’s knot, which occur when $b=0$ (which is not possible, by assumption) and $b\in\{4,-5\}$ , respectively; hence $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if $L$ is isotopic to $P(1,1,-1)$ , $P(1,1,-5)$ , or $P(1,1,4)$ . The first two links belong to the last two bullet points listed in the statement of the lemma; the last link belongs to the first bullet point.

We now assume that $a,b\not\in\{-1,1\}$ . It is easy to see that $L$ is isotopic to the two-bridge link $C(a+1,b+1)=K(-ab-a-b,b+1)$ ; see Figure 5.

*Figure 5. The pretzel link $P(1,a,b)$ is isotopic to the 2-bridge link $C(a+1,b+1)=K(-ab-a-b,b+1)$ .*

First suppose $a$ and $b$ have opposite sign. Up to mirroring and isotoping, we may assume that $a<-1$ and $b>1$ . Then $\frac{-ab-a-b}{b+1}=[-a,2^{[b]}]^{-}$ . Following as in the proof of Lemma 2.3, it is clear that $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if either $-a=b$ or $-a=b+4$ , which yield the links in the third and fourth bullet points in the statement of the lemma.

Next assume $a$ and $b$ have the same sign. Up to mirroring an isotoping, we may assume that $a,b<-1$ . First suppose $a=-2$ or $b=-2$ ; up to isotopy, we may assume the latter. Since $\det L\neq 0$ , it follows that $a<-2$ . If $a=-3$ , then it is easy to see that $L$ is the unknot; hence $P(1,-3,-2)=P(1,-2,-3)$ is $\chi-$ slice. Assume $a<-3$ . Then $\frac{-ab-a-b}{b+1}=-(a+2)=[-(a+2)]^{-}$ and $(-(a+2))$ has dual $(2^{[-(a+3)]})$ . Following as in the proof of Lemma 2.3, it is clear that $L$ is $\chi-$ slice if and only if $a=-6$ ; that is, $L$ is isotopic to $P(1,-6,-2)=P(1,-2,-6)$ . Finally suppose $a,b<-2$ . Then $\frac{-ab-a-b}{b+1}=[-(a+1),-(b+1)]^{-}$ and $(-(a+1),-(b+1))$ has dual $(2^{[-(a+3)]},3,2^{[-(b+3)]})$ . Arguing as above, it is clear that $L$ if $\chi-$ slice if and only if $a=-6$ and $b=-3$ (or vice versa); that is, $L$ is isotopic to $P(1,-3,-6)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 2.5.

$P(1,1,a,b)$ , where $a<0$ and $b>0$ , is $\chi-$ slice (and $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if $(a,b)\in\{(-1,3),(3,-4)\}$ .

#### Proof.

First suppose $b=1$ . Then it is easy to see that $P(1,1,a,1)=P(1,1,1,a)$ is the 2-bridge link $C(3,a)=K(3a+1,a)$ and that $[3,-a]^{-}=\frac{3a+1}{a}$ . Notice that the string $(3,-a)$ has dual $(2,3,2^{[-a-2]})$ . We can see that neither of these strings fall under Theorem 2.1; hence $P(1,1,1,a)$ is not $\chi$ -slice for all $a\leq-1$ .

Next assume $b\geq 2$ . Figure 6 shows that $P(1,1,a,b)=P(b,1,1,a)$ is the 2-bridge link $L=C(-b,-2,-a)$ . First suppose $a=-1$ ; then it is easy to see that $L$ is isotopic to the torus link $T(2,b+1)$ . By Corollary 2.2, $L$ is $\chi-$ slice (and, indeed $\chi-$ ribbon) if and only if $b=3$ . Next suppose $a\leq-2$ . and consider $-L=C(b,2,a)=K(2ab+a+b,2a+1)$ . It is routine to check that $[b+1,3,2^{[-a-2]}]^{-}=\frac{2ab+a+b}{2a+1}$ . Note that the dual of $(b+1,3,2^{[-a-2]})$ is $(2^{[b-1]},3,-a)$ . Consider the list of strings in Theorem 2.1. Up to reversal, neither $(b+1,3,2^{[-a-2]})$ nor $(2^{[b-1]},3,-a)$ are of the form $(a)-(d)$ or $(f)$ . They are of the form $(e)$ and $(f)$ precisely when $x=y=0$ , yielding $(a,b)=(-4,3)$ . ∎

### 2.2. $\chi-$ slice pretzel links

We now describe the standard method for showing that a link is $\chi-$ slice. A ribbon (or band) move is an operation on a link diagram illustrated in Figure 7. Given a ribbon (or band), an embedding $f:I\times I\to S^{3}-L$ with $f(\{0,1\}\times I)\subset L$ , a new link is formed as $L^{\prime}=(L-f(\{0,1\}\times I))\cup f(I\times\{0,1\}).$ We say that $L^{\prime}$ is obtained from $L$ by a ribbon (or band) move. It is an elementary argument to show the following proposition.

*Figure 7. Obtaining a new link $L^{\prime}$ from $L$ via a ribbon (band) move using the band $B$ .*

#### Proposition 2.6.

If $L$ admits a sequence of $n$ ribbon moves which convert $L$ to the split union of an $n$ -component unlink and a $\chi-$ slice link $L^{\prime}$ , then $L$ is $\chi-$ slice. Moreover, if $L^{\prime}$ is $\chi-$ ribbon, then $L$ is also $\chi-$ ribbon.

We first prove that the positive pretzel links listed in Theorem 1.3 are indeed $\chi-$ ribbon.

#### Proposition 2.7.

The positive pretzel links $P(2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2)$ and $P(1^{[z]},2^{[2k]},k+z\pm 2)$ (and their mirrors) are $\chi-$ ribbon.

#### Proof.

Performing $k$ band moves to the pretzel link $P(1^{[z]},2^{[2k]},k+z\pm 2)$ , as indicated in Figure 8, yields the split union of the unlink of $k$ components and the pretzel link $P(1^{[k+z]},k+z\pm 2)$ , which is $\chi-$ ribbon by Lemma 2.3. Similarly, performing four band moves to $P(2,2,2,2,2,2,2)$ , as indicated in Figure 8 yields the split union of the unlink of four components and the torus link $T(2,-4)$ , which is $\chi-$ ribbon by Corollary 2.2. The result now follows from Proposition 2.6. ∎
